Make each expression as concise as possible.
The less clutter an expression has, the easier it is to read.
This is one case of [building every unit from smaller atomic units](teaching.qmd#build-every-unit-from-smaller-atomic-units).

Before you finish a definition, theorem or proof,
scan it for a sub-expression that is written out in full
more than once,
or that is a conceptually coherent chunk
even if it appears only once,
such as the prediction error (the fitted value minus the outcome)
or the loss of a prediction on one observation.
Give the chunk a name and a macro,
and write the macro everywhere the chunk appears.

::: {#exm-concise-expression}

## Naming a repeated chunk

> ❌ Source: `The loss is $\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \paren{\eoutvar_i - \outvar_i}^2$, and its derivative is $\frac{2}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \paren{\eoutvar_i - \outvar_i} \predvar_i$.`
>
> ✅ Source: `The loss is $\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \prederr_i^2$, and its derivative is $\frac{2}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \prederr_i \predvar_i$.`

Both versions print the same quantities.
The ❌ version writes the difference `\eoutvar_i - \outvar_i` out twice.
The ✅ version names it once, as the prediction error,
and each formula shows at a glance what it is built from.

:::

Write each expression in its most compact form,
built from named sub-pieces that are defined separately.
Use one form per expression, and keep it simple.
For example, write the expected squared error
as the squared bias plus the [variance](#def-variance) plus the residual variance,
and define each of the three pieces on its own,
instead of expanding them inside the formula.

Search the shared macros for the chunk before you write it by hand.
A macro often exists already,
and any expression spelled out in full that a macro or a shorter form could say
is the sign that nobody looked.
A difference is only the commonest case.
For example, an exercise wrote the left side of the bias--variance decomposition as
`\E{\paren{\newoutvar - \predvalf{\newpredval}}^2}`,
when `\prederrf{\predvalf{\newpredval}}` names the same prediction error,
and the squared bias, written out the same way, has `\biassymf`.
When you find one such chunk, sweep the other notes repositories for it,
in small batches of one repository each.

Add the macro to the shared macro file before you use it,
never as a local macro in one document
(see [Using shared macros](#using-shared-macros)),
and record its meaning in that file's `interpretations.tsv`.
